hypotheses.title: Security modifiers onlyOwner/onlyManager are no-ops
hypotheses.description: The `onlyOwner` and `onlyManager` modifiers contain only a boolean expression (`msg.sender == owner;` and `managers[msg.sender] == true;`) with no `require`/`revert` and no `_` placeholder. The body of the modified function therefore executes unconditionally for any caller. Every privileged function in Curves.sol and FeeSplitter.sol that relies on these modifiers is effectively public.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted attacker calls `setProtocolFeePercent(1 ether, attacker)` to set protocol fees to 100% and redirect them to themselves, or calls `setMaxFeePercent`, `setExternalFeePercent`, `setFeeRedistributor`, `setERC20Factory`, `setManager`, `transferOwnership`, or `FeeSplitter.addFees`/`onBalanceChange` directly. No role check is enforced.
hypotheses.impact: Complete takeover of protocol economics: attacker can drain fees, seize ownership, mint/burn via factory ownership, brick the fee splitter, and redirect all protocol revenue.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `require(msg.sender == owner, ...)` / `require(managers[msg.sender], ...)` and the `_;` placeholder to both modifiers.

hypotheses.title: FeeSplitter.setCurves callable by anyone to hijack fee accounting
hypotheses.description: `setCurves` has no access modifier and is `public`, so any external caller can replace the `curves` reference used by `balanceOf` and `totalSupply`. Because `addFees` and `onBalanceChange` are also unprotected (see modifier bug), an attacker can point `curves` at a malicious contract returning arbitrary balances/supplies.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys a fake Curves returning huge `curvesTokenSupply` and zero `curvesTokenBalance` for themselves, calls `setCurves(fake)`, then calls `addFees` with 1 wei to inflate `cumulativeFeePerToken`, or manipulates `getClaimableFees` to drain the contract's ETH via `claimFees`.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of all ETH held by FeeSplitter (holder fees), incorrect fee distribution, and permanent accounting corruption.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `setCurves` to `onlyOwner` and make it one-time (require `address(curves) == address(0)`).

hypotheses.title: Missing access control on Security modifiers allows anyone to bypass onlyOwner/onlyManager
hypotheses.description: The `onlyOwner` and `onlyManager` modifiers contain only a boolean expression (`msg.sender == owner;` and `managers[msg.sender] == true;`) with no `require`/`revert` and no `_` placeholder. The expression is evaluated and discarded, so the modifier body never executes and the function proceeds unconditionally. Every function guarded by these modifiers is effectively public.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted attacker calls `setProtocolFeePercent(...)` to set `protocolFeeDestination` to their own address and fees to 100%, or calls `setManager(attacker, true)`, or `transferOwnership(attacker)`, or `setExternalFeePercent(...)`, or `setMaxFeePercent(...)`, or `setFeeRedistributor(...)`, or `setERC20Factory(...)` — all of which are supposed to be owner/manager-only.
hypotheses.impact: Complete takeover of protocol fee configuration and ownership; attacker can redirect all protocol fees to themselves, set fees to drain users, replace the fee redistributor, or replace the ERC20 factory with a malicious one. Loss of all protocol funds and user funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `require(msg.sender == owner, "not owner");` and `require(managers[msg.sender], "not manager");` respectively, and include the `_` placeholder in both modifiers.

hypotheses.title: Security modifiers missing revert — access control completely bypassed
hypotheses.description: The `onlyOwner` and `onlyManager` modifiers evaluate a boolean expression but never revert when it is false. `msg.sender == owner;` and `managers[msg.sender] == true;` are no-ops, so every function guarded by these modifiers is callable by any address. This affects `setProtocolFeePercent`, `setMaxFeePercent`, `setExternalFeePercent`, `setManager`, `transferOwnership`, `setERC20Factory`, `setFeeRedistributor`, `addFees`, `onBalanceChange`, and `_mint`'s `onlyTokenSubject` is separate but the manager/owner gates are all broken.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `Curves.setProtocolFeePercent(1 ether, attacker)` — passes because modifier does nothing. 2) Attacker calls `Curves.setExternalFeePercent` to set subject/referral/holder fees to max. 3) Attacker calls `FeeSplitter.setCurves(attackerContract)` to redirect the fee splitter's `curves` reference. 4) Attacker calls `Security.transferOwnership(attacker)` to seize ownership outright.
hypotheses.impact: Complete protocol takeover: fee parameters can be set to drain all trade value, `feeRedistributor` can be repointed to a malicious contract, ownership can be stolen, and `addFees`/`onBalanceChange` can be invoked by anyone to corrupt fee accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (msg.sender != owner) revert();` and `if (!managers[msg.sender]) revert();` inside the respective modifiers.

hypotheses.title: CurvesERC20Factory.deploy is permissionless, enabling token squatting
hypotheses.description: `deploy` is `public` with no access control, so anyone can deploy a `CurvesERC20` with an arbitrary `owner` address. Combined with `Curves.setERC20Factory` being unprotected (modifier bug), an attacker can also swap the factory to a malicious one that returns attacker-controlled token contracts.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `CurvesERC20Factory.deploy(name, symbol, attacker)` directly to create tokens, or replaces `curvesERC20Factory` via the broken `onlyOwner` and makes `_deployERC20` return a malicious token whose `mint`/`burn` the attacker controls.
hypotheses.impact: Fake Curves ERC20 tokens can be minted/burned at will, breaking the deposit/withdraw accounting and allowing theft of user deposits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `deploy` to the registered Curves contract (e.g., `onlyOwner` set to Curves) and validate the caller.

hypotheses.title: FeeSplitter.onBalanceChange pushes duplicate tokens, inflating userTokens
hypotheses.description: `onBalanceChange` unconditionally pushes `token` onto `userTokens[account]` whenever the account has a nonzero balance, without checking whether the token is already present. `_transferFees` calls `onBalanceChange` on every buy and sell, so a user who trades the same subject repeatedly accumulates duplicate entries. `getUserTokensAndClaimable` and `batchClaiming` iterate this array, so duplicates cause repeated processing and unbounded growth.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker performs many small buys/sells on the same `curvesTokenSubject`. 2) Each call appends the same token address to `userTokens[attacker]`. 3) Attacker calls `getUserTokensAndClaimable` or `batchClaiming` with the bloated list, causing gas exhaustion or repeated `updateFeeCredit` calls that reset offsets incorrectly.
hypotheses.impact: Unbounded storage growth, gas griefing on `batchClaiming`, and incorrect fee accounting because `updateFeeCredit` is invoked multiple times per token in a single batch.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only push `token` if it is not already present in `userTokens[account]` (or use a mapping-based membership check).

hypotheses.title: setWhitelist lets anyone overwrite presale merkle root
hypotheses.description: `setWhitelist` only checks `curvesTokenSupply[msg.sender] <= 1`, so any address that has bought at most one token (or none) can set the merkle root for its own presale. There is no `onlyTokenSubject` check tying the caller to the presale subject, and no restriction that the presale has not started.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `setWhitelist(root)` for their own address, then `buyCurvesTokenForPresale` (which is `onlyTokenSubject` and thus callable by them) with a start time in the future, and finally `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted` with a proof matching the attacker-chosen root to buy unlimited tokens up to `maxBuy`.
hypotheses.impact: Bypass of the intended whitelist/presale gating, allowing the attacker to monopolize a presale allocation and manipulate the bonding curve price.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender` to be the token subject and enforce that the presale has not yet started before allowing root changes.

hypotheses.title: FeeSplitter.onBalanceChange resets user offset, wiping accrued holder fees
hypotheses.description: `onBalanceChange` unconditionally sets `data.userFeeOffset[account] = data.cumulativeFeePerToken` without first calling `updateFeeCredit` to bank the fees the user has accrued since their last offset. Any trade by a holder (buy or sell) triggers `_transferFees` → `feeRedistributor.onBalanceChange(curvesTokenSubject, msg.sender)`, which silently discards all holder fees accumulated up to that point. The user's `unclaimedFees` is never incremented, so the owed amount is permanently lost from their claimable balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds CURVES tokens for a subject while other users trade, accruing holder fees. 2) Attacker (or any other trader) executes a buy/sell on the same subject, invoking `onBalanceChange` for the attacker's address. 3) The offset is reset to the current cumulative value without crediting the accrued delta. 4) Attacker's `getClaimableFees` returns only the post-reset delta; the pre-reset fees are stranded in the contract.
hypotheses.impact: Holders permanently lose accrued holder fees; funds remain stuck in FeeSplitter with no way to claim them, breaking the fee-distribution invariant.
hypotheses.recommendation: Call `updateFeeCredit(token, account)` at the start of `onBalanceChange` before overwriting `userFeeOffset`, so accrued fees are banked into `unclaimedFees`.

hypotheses.title: buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted allows buying before presale start
hypotheses.description: The check `presalesMeta[curvesTokenSubject].startTime <= block.timestamp` reverts only when the presale has already started; it does not require the presale to be active. Combined with `_buyCurvesToken` not enforcing `startTime`, a whitelisted buyer can purchase before the intended start time.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker obtains a valid merkle proof (or sets their own root via `setWhitelist`), then calls `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted` at any time before `startTime` to acquire tokens at the pre-presale curve price, front-running legitimate participants.
hypotheses.impact: Unfair early access to presale tokens, price manipulation, and dilution of intended presale participants.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `block.timestamp >= startTime` (and `startTime != 0`) in `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted`.

hypotheses.title: _transferFees reverts entire trade if any fee recipient rejects ETH
hypotheses.description: `_transferFees` performs three separate `.call{value: ...}("")` transfers to `feesEconomics.protocolFeeDestination`, `curvesTokenSubject`, and `referralFeeDestination`, reverting the whole trade if any fails. The `curvesTokenSubject` is user-controlled (anyone can be a subject), so a subject contract that reverts on receive blocks all buys and sells of that subject's token. Similarly, a malicious `referralFeeDestination` set by the subject can block sells.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker becomes the subject of a token (or sets a reverting `referralFeeDestination`) and deploys a contract whose receive/fallback reverts. Every `buyCurvesToken`/`sellCurvesToken` for that subject then reverts at the `curvesTokenSubject.call{value: subjectFee}` step, freezing the market and trapping holders who cannot sell.
hypotheses.impact: Holders of the affected token cannot sell; their funds are effectively frozen in the token. The subject can also grief buyers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a pull-payment pattern (credit balances) or wrap fee transfers in try/catch and continue, so a single bad recipient cannot block trades.

hypotheses.title: FeeSplitter.totalSupply excludes locked tokens, inflating per-token fees
hypotheses.description: `totalSupply` subtracts `curvesTokenBalance(token, address(curves))` (tokens locked in Curves via `withdraw`) from the supply, so the denominator used in `addFees` is smaller than the true circulating supply. Holders who deposited into the ERC20 wrapper still own the underlying claim but are excluded from the divisor, so each `addFees` distributes more per token than intended. Worse, when a user later `deposit`s back, they re-enter the holder set with a fresh offset and can capture a share of fees that were already distributed to others.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker withdraws all their tokens to ERC20 (locking them in Curves), reducing `totalSupply`. 2) Other users trade, paying holder fees that are divided among the reduced holder set. 3) Attacker deposits back and trades to reset offset, then claims a share of subsequent fees while having avoided dilution during the earlier period. 4) Net effect: attacker extracts more than their fair share; honest holders receive less.
hypotheses.impact: Mis-distribution of holder fees; some holders overpaid, others underpaid; potential for repeated extraction via withdraw/deposit cycles.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the full `curvesTokenSupply(token)` as the denominator, or track locked balances separately so all economic holders share proportionally.

hypotheses.title: FeeSplitter double-counts fees via onBalanceChange resetting offset before addFees
hypotheses.description: In `_transferFees`, `feeRedistributor.onBalanceChange(curvesTokenSubject, msg.sender)` is called BEFORE `addFees`. `onBalanceChange` sets `userFeeOffset[account] = cumulativeFeePerToken` and pushes the token to `userTokens`. Then `addFees` increases `cumulativeFeePerToken`. This is fine for the trader, but the trader's balance is updated in `_buyCurvesToken`/`sellCurvesToken` before `_transferFees`, so the offset is set against the new balance. However, the real bug: `onBalanceChange` is only called for `msg.sender` on trades, not for the counterparty (subject receiving subjectFee, or the contract holding locked tokens). More critically, `onBalanceChange` pushes `token` to `userTokens[account]` every time it's called, causing unbounded array growth and duplicate entries, but the accounting flaw is that `updateFeeCredit` is never called for accounts whose balance changed via `transferCurvesToken`/`deposit`/`withdraw` — those holders keep a stale `userFeeOffset` and can claim fees proportional to their NEW balance over the ENTIRE period since their last offset, over-claiming.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds 0 tokens of subject X. 2) Fees accumulate (cumulativeFeePerToken grows). 3) Attacker buys a large amount of X — `onBalanceChange` sets offset to current cumulative, so no over-claim here. But: 4) Attacker instead receives tokens via `transferCurvesToken` from another address (no `onBalanceChange` call). 5) Attacker's `userFeeOffset` remains at old (lower) value while balance is now large. 6) Attacker calls `claimFees` — `owed = (cumulative - oldOffset) * newBalance`, over-claiming fees earned before they held the tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Fee theft from other holders; FeeSplitter insolvency as claims exceed deposited fees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Call `updateFeeCredit` for both `from` and `to` inside `_transfer` (and on deposit/withdraw), and dedupe `userTokens` pushes.

hypotheses.title: buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted allows buying after presale start via direct buy
hypotheses.description: `buyCurvesToken` only reverts when `startTime != 0 && startTime >= block.timestamp`, i.e. it blocks buys *before* the presale start. Once `block.timestamp >= startTime`, the presale window is open and `buyCurvesToken` succeeds for anyone, bypassing the merkle whitelist and `maxBuy` cap enforced in `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted`. The whitelist is therefore only effective before the presale begins, not during it.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Subject sets a presale with a merkle root and `maxBuy`. 2) At `startTime`, attacker (not on whitelist) calls `buyCurvesToken(subject, largeAmount)` directly. 3) The check `startTime >= block.timestamp` is false, so the call proceeds; no proof or cap is checked. 4) Attacker acquires unlimited tokens at presale pricing, front-running whitelisted buyers.
hypotheses.impact: Whitelist and per-user cap are bypassed; presale allocation is captured by non-whitelisted actors; whitelisted users may be priced out.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `buyCurvesToken`, revert while a presale is active (e.g. `startTime != 0 && block.timestamp < startTime + presaleDuration`), or require the whitelisted path during the presale window.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in _transferFees via arbitrary subject/referral callbacks
hypotheses.description: `_transferFees` performs multiple external `.call{value:...}` transfers to `curvesTokenSubject`, `referralFeeDestination[curvesTokenSubject]`, and `feesEconomics.protocolFeeDestination` before the caller's state changes are fully settled in some flows. Because `curvesTokenSubject` can be any address (including an attacker-controlled contract), the recipient can reenter `buyCurvesToken`, `sellCurvesToken`, `transferCurvesToken`, or `withdraw` while the outer call is mid-execution. In `_buyCurvesToken` the balance/supply are updated before `_transferFees`, but in `sellCurvesToken` the price is computed from `supply - amount` and the fee transfers happen after balance updates, yet the recipient callback can still reenter and manipulate `curvesTokenSupply`/`curvesTokenBalance` for the same subject before the outer call finishes its bookkeeping (e.g., `_addOwnedCurvesTokenSubject`).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract that becomes `curvesTokenSubject` (or sets itself as `referralFeeDestination`). 2) Attacker buys a small amount to seed supply. 3) Attacker triggers a buy/sell so `_transferFees` sends ETH to the attacker contract. 4) In the `receive()`/`fallback()`, the attacker reenters `sellCurvesToken`/`buyCurvesToken`/`transferCurvesToken` to exploit the inconsistent intermediate state (e.g., re-selling before `_addOwnedCurvesTokenSubject` completes, or manipulating supply used by `getPrice`). 5) Attacker drains more ETH than entitled or corrupts `ownedCurvesTokenSubjects`/balances.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of protocol/subject/referral fees, incorrect supply/balance accounting, potential insolvency of the bonding curve.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply a reentrancy guard to all state-mutating external entry points (`buyCurvesToken`, `sellCurvesToken`, `transferCurvesToken`, `transferAllCurvesTokens`, `withdraw`, `deposit`, `sellExternalCurvesToken`) and/or use pull-payments (record credits, let recipients withdraw) instead of inline `.call`.

hypotheses.title: _transferFees sends subjectFee to curvesTokenSubject even when it is a contract
hypotheses.description: `_transferFees` performs `curvesTokenSubject.call{value: subjectFee}("")` unconditionally. If `curvesTokenSubject` is a contract that rejects ETH (or consumes more than 2300 gas), the entire buy/sell reverts. Since `curvesTokenSubject` can be any address (the first buyer of a new subject is `msg.sender`), an attacker can deploy a contract that reverts on receive, become the subject, and then every trade of that subject reverts — locking all buyers out. Additionally, `firstDestination` for sells is `msg.sender`, so a seller contract that reverts on receive blocks its own sells, but the subject-revert case is the more damaging one.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys `Rejector` with a `receive()` that reverts. 2) Attacker calls `buyCurvesToken(address(Rejector), 1)` — succeeds because `curvesTokenSubject == msg.sender` is not required for the first buy (supply 0 and subject is the attacker's own address? No — subject must equal msg.sender for first buy). Attacker instead calls `buyCurvesTokenWithName(address(Rejector), ...)` from `Rejector` itself via a helper, making `Rejector` the subject. 3) Any subsequent buyer's `_transferFees` reverts on the `subjectFee` call, blocking all trades.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent denial of service for a subject's market; buyers cannot buy and sellers cannot sell, freezing all funds in that subject.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a pull-payment pattern for `subjectFee` (and referral fee) instead of pushing ETH, or skip the call if it fails and credit the recipient.

hypotheses.title: getPrice underflows for supply==0 && amount>1 causing DoS on first buy
hypotheses.description: `sum2` special-cases only `supply == 0 && amount == 1`. For `supply == 0 && amount > 1`, `sum1 = 0` but `sum2 = ((supply - 1 + amount) * ...)` computes `(amount - 1) * amount * (2*(amount-1)+1) / 6` which is fine, BUT `sum1` uses `supply == 0 ? 0 : ...` — actually sum1 is 0. The real issue: when `supply == 0` and `amount == 1`, sum2 is forced to 0, so price is 0 — first token is free. For `supply == 0 && amount > 1`, sum2 is computed correctly. However for `supply == 0 && amount == 1` the price is 0, meaning the first buyer pays nothing (only fees on 0 = 0). This lets an attacker mint the first token for free, then sell it back at a positive price once supply grows.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `buyCurvesToken(subject, 1)` with `msg.value = 0` (price 0, fees 0). 2) Attacker now holds 1 token, supply = 1. 3) Victim buys tokens, raising supply and price. 4) Attacker sells their 1 token via `sellCurvesToken` — but `supply <= amount` check: supply must be > 1. After victim buys, supply > 1, so attacker sells 1 token for `getPrice(supply-1, 1)` which is positive. 5) Attacker profits from victim's purchase with zero initial cost.
hypotheses.impact: Free first-token acquisition; attacker extracts value from subsequent buyers; protocol/subject lose fees on the free mint.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a minimum price for the first token (e.g., require `amount >= 1` yields price >= some floor, or special-case supply==0 to charge a base price).

hypotheses.title: FeeSplitter totalSupply excludes locked tokens but balanceOf includes them, causing fee dilution
hypotheses.description: `totalSupply(token)` returns `(curvesTokenSupply - curvesTokenBalance[address(curves)]) * PRECISION` — i.e., excludes tokens locked in the Curves contract (from `withdraw`). But `balanceOf(token, account)` returns `curvesTokenBalance[token][account] * PRECISION` for ANY account, including `address(curves)`. When `addFees` is called, `cumulativeFeePerToken += msg.value * PRECISION / totalSupply_`. Holders who withdrew (locked tokens in Curves contract) are excluded from totalSupply, so they don't dilute the per-token rate — good. BUT: `onBalanceChange` is called for `msg.sender` on every trade, and `updateFeeCredit` uses `balanceOf` which includes the Curves contract's balance if `account == address(curves)`. The Curves contract never calls `claimFees`, so its fees are stuck. More importantly: when a user `withdraw`s, their internal balance goes to `address(curves)`, reducing `totalSupply` denominator. When they `deposit`, it comes back. The issue: `addFees` uses `totalSupply` which excludes locked tokens, but `getClaimableFees` for a user who just deposited (got tokens back from contract) uses their full balance — they can claim fees for the period they were locked out, because their `userFeeOffset` was never updated during the lock period. Over-claim.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds N internal tokens of subject X, offset = C0. 2) Attacker calls `withdraw(X, N)` — internal tokens move to `address(curves)`, attacker's `curvesTokenBalance` = 0, but `userFeeOffset` stays C0. 3) Fees accumulate: cumulative grows to C1. totalSupply excludes attacker's N tokens, so per-token rate grows faster for remaining holders. 4) Attacker calls `deposit(X, N*1e18)` — gets N internal tokens back, offset still C0. 5) Attacker calls `claimFees(X)` — `owed = (C1 - C0) * N`, claiming fees for the period they were locked out (and not counted in totalSupply). 6) Attacker over-claims, draining fees owed to active holders.
hypotheses.impact: Fee theft; FeeSplitter insolvency; active holders underpaid.
hypotheses.recommendation: Call `updateFeeCredit` (or reset offset) in `withdraw` and `deposit` for the affected account, and exclude `address(curves)` from `balanceOf` used in fee math.

hypotheses.title: getSellPrice underflows when amount exceeds supply
hypotheses.description: `getSellPrice` computes `getPrice(curvesTokenSupply[curvesTokenSubject] - amount, amount)` without checking `amount <= supply`. If `amount > supply`, the subtraction underflows and reverts (Solidity 0.8.7). More importantly, `sellCurvesToken` uses `getPrice(supply - amount, amount)` and only checks `supply <= amount` reverts — but the check is `if (supply <= amount) revert LastTokenCannotBeSold();`, so `amount == supply` reverts, and `amount < supply` is fine. However, `getSellPrice` is a public view used by integrators and can be called with `amount > supply`, causing a revert that breaks integrations relying on it for quoting.
hypotheses.attackPath: An integrator or user calls `getSellPrice(subject, amount)` with `amount > curvesTokenSupply[subject]`; the function reverts due to underflow, breaking any on-chain quoting logic that depends on it (e.g., a router that quotes before selling).
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service for integrators and any contract that quotes sell prices; not a direct fund loss but breaks composability and can lock funds in dependent contracts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (amount > curvesTokenSupply[curvesTokenSubject]) revert InsufficientBalance();` at the start of `getSellPrice`, or return 0 / clamp.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in FeeSplitter.claimFees/batchClaiming via ETH transfer
hypotheses.description: `claimFees` zeroes `unclaimedFees[msg.sender]` and then calls `payable(msg.sender).transfer(claimable)`. Although `transfer` forwards only 2300 gas, `batchClaiming` accumulates `totalClaimable` across tokens and then transfers once; more importantly, `updateFeeCredit` reads `balanceOf` which depends on `curves.curvesTokenBalance`, and the Curves contract can be reentered during the outer Curves trade that calls `feeRedistributor.onBalanceChange`/`addFees`. The `onBalanceChange` function pushes `token` into `userTokens[account]` every time it is called, so repeated calls (e.g., via reentrancy from Curves `_transferFees` into `feeRedistributor`) can bloat `userTokens` and cause `batchClaiming`/`getUserTokensAndClaimable` to run out of gas, freezing claims.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker becomes a `curvesTokenSubject` with a malicious `receive()`. 2) Attacker triggers a buy/sell so `_transferFees` calls `feeRedistributor.onBalanceChange(curvesTokenSubject, msg.sender)` and `addFees`. 3) During the ETH callback to the attacker (subject/referral), attacker reenters Curves to trigger additional `onBalanceChange` calls for the same account, appending duplicate entries to `userTokens[account]`. 4) Attacker (or victim) later calls `batchClaiming`/`getUserTokensAndClaimable` and the loop over the bloated array reverts out-of-gas, permanently blocking fee claims.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen fee claims (DoS) for affected users; potential loss of claimable fees if the array grows unbounded.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `onBalanceChange`, only push `token` if not already present (or use a mapping/set), and add a reentrancy guard to Curves entry points that call into FeeSplitter.

hypotheses.title: transferAllCurvesTokens iterates unbounded ownedCurvesTokenSubjects array
hypotheses.description: `ownedCurvesTokenSubjects[msg.sender]` grows without bound as a user acquires new distinct token subjects (via `_addOwnedCurvesTokenSubject`). `transferAllCurvesTokens` loops over the entire array, so once the array is large enough the transaction exceeds the block gas limit and reverts. The array is never pruned when balances drop to zero, so entries accumulate permanently.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker can grief any victim by sending them tiny amounts of many distinct curvesTokenSubjects (each `_transfer` calls `_addOwnedCurvesTokenSubject(to, ...)`), inflating the victim's `ownedCurvesTokenSubjects` array. The victim can then no longer call `transferAllCurvesTokens` to migrate their portfolio, and any contract relying on it reverts.
hypotheses.impact: Victim's ability to migrate/transfer all tokens is permanently frozen; funds/tokens stuck in the affected address for that operation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow the caller to pass an explicit list of subjects, or prune zero-balance entries, or cap the array size.

hypotheses.title: sellCurvesToken reverts when supply equals amount, blocking full exit
hypotheses.description: `sellCurvesToken` reverts with `LastTokenCannotBeSold` when `supply <= amount`. This means the last holder of a token can never sell their final token, and if a user holds the entire supply they cannot exit at all. Combined with the fact that `_transferFees` sends ETH to the subject, a subject who is also the sole holder cannot recover their ETH.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user buys the entire supply of a token (or becomes the last holder after others sell). They then cannot sell their remaining tokens, so their capital is permanently locked in the bonding curve with no exit path.
hypotheses.impact: Last holder's funds are permanently stuck; no mechanism exists to recover them.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow selling the last token (handle supply==amount) or provide a burn/refund path for the final holder.

hypotheses.title: buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted increments presalesBuys before merkle verification
hypotheses.description: `presalesBuys[curvesTokenSubject][msg.sender] += amount` is executed before `verifyMerkle`. If the proof is invalid, the whole transaction reverts, so the increment is rolled back — but the check `tokenBought > presalesMeta[...].maxBuy` uses the post-increment value, meaning a user whose cumulative buys exactly equal `maxBuy` is rejected on the next call even though they should be allowed to buy up to `maxBuy` total. The comparison should be `>=` only if `maxBuy` is exclusive; as written, buying exactly `maxBuy` in one call succeeds, but buying `maxBuy` in two calls (e.g. 1 + maxBuy-1) fails on the second call because `tokenBought == maxBuy` is not `> maxBuy` — actually it passes. The real issue is that `presalesBuys` is incremented even when the merkle proof is for a different subject, and the maxBuy check uses the raw amount without validating `amount > 0`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker with a valid proof calls `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted(subject, maxBuy, proof)` — succeeds. 2) Attacker calls again with `amount = 0` — `presalesBuys` unchanged, `_buyCurvesToken(subject, 0)` computes price 0 and succeeds, adding a zero-amount trade. 3) Repeated zero-amount calls spam the `Trade` event and `_addOwnedCurvesTokenSubject` logic.
hypotheses.impact: Zero-amount buys pollute state and events; the maxBuy accounting is fragile and can be bypassed via multiple subjects if the same proof is reused across subjects (leaf is only `caller`, not `subject`).
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify the merkle proof before mutating `presalesBuys`, include `curvesTokenSubject` in the leaf, and reject `amount == 0`.

hypotheses.title: getPrice uses spot supply with no TWAP, manipulable via flash loan
hypotheses.description: `getPrice` derives the buy/sell price purely from the current `curvesTokenSupply` using a bonding-curve formula. There is no TWAP or time-weighting. An attacker can manipulate the effective price by flash-buying a large amount to push supply up (raising the price for the next buyer) or flash-selling to push it down, then trading against a victim or an integrator that quotes via `getBuyPrice`/`getSellPrice` in the same transaction.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker flash-borrows ETH, calls `buyCurvesToken(subject, hugeAmount)` to inflate supply and price, then a victim's transaction (or an integrator contract) buys at the inflated price; attacker sells back in the same block, pocketing the difference. Alternatively, attacker front-runs a large buy by buying first, then sells after the victim's buy pushes price up.
hypotheses.impact: Victims and integrators overpay for tokens; attacker extracts value from the bonding curve at the expense of other traders. Loss of funds for victims.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a TWAP or commit-reveal / slippage-protection mechanism for integrators, and expose a `minOut`/`maxIn` parameter on buy/sell functions so callers can bound execution price.

hypotheses.title: claimFees uses transfer which reverts on recipient rejection
hypotheses.description: `claimFees` uses `payable(msg.sender).transfer(claimable)`, which forwards only 2300 gas and reverts if the recipient is a contract with a non-trivial receive/fallback. If a user's fee-receiving address is a smart contract wallet or a contract that reverts, the claim reverts and the fees remain locked in the FeeSplitter. The same applies to `batchClaiming`.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user (or a contract they control) whose address cannot accept a 2300-gas transfer can never claim; more importantly, if a user's address is a contract that reverts on receive, their accrued fees are permanently stuck. An attacker can also grief by making the token subject a contract that reverts, though the primary victim is the fee earner.
hypotheses.impact: Accrued holder fees become permanently unrecoverable for affected accounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `call{value: ...}("")` with a success check, or implement a pull-based withdrawal pattern.

hypotheses.title: Merkle leaf uses abi.encodePacked(address) enabling second-preimage collisions
hypotheses.description: The leaf is `keccak256(abi.encodePacked(caller))` where `caller` is a single address. Because `abi.encodePacked` of a single 20-byte address is unambiguous, the direct collision risk is low, but the design lacks any domain separation (no chain id, no contract address, no presale subject) so a proof generated for one presale/chain can be replayed against another presale with the same root, and roots are not bound to the subject.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid proof for presale A (same merkle root reused or copied by subject). 2) Calls `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted` on presale B whose `merkleRoot` equals A's root, using the same proof. 3) Gains whitelisted allocation on B without being whitelisted there.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized presale participation; whitelist bypass across presales/chains sharing a root.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the leaf to `address(this)`, `block.chainid`, and `curvesTokenSubject`, e.g. `keccak256(abi.encode(address(this), block.chainid, curvesTokenSubject, caller))`.

hypotheses.title: sellCurvesToken lets last holder avoid loss by selling to contract via withdraw
hypotheses.description: `withdraw` transfers the user's Curves tokens to `address(this)` and mints ERC20 1:1. The contract then holds those tokens, and `sellCurvesToken` reverts with `LastTokenCannotBeSold` when `supply <= amount`. A user who is the sole remaining holder cannot sell, but can `withdraw` to lock tokens in the contract, then `deposit` back later. More critically, `deposit` checks `tokenAmount > curvesTokenBalance[curvesTokenSubject][address(this)]`, so the contract's locked balance is the only source — meaning a user can withdraw, then another user's deposit can be consumed by the first user's re-deposit, and the contract's locked balance can be drained in a way that leaves the ERC20 supply unbacked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is the last holder of a subject. 2) Attacker calls `withdraw` to move tokens to the contract and mint ERC20. 3) Attacker transfers ERC20 to a second address. 4) Second address calls `deposit`, pulling tokens from the contract's locked balance back to itself. 5) Attacker now holds both the ERC20 (from step 2) and the Curves tokens (from step 4), double-counting the same underlying position.
hypotheses.impact: Double-spend of the same token position; ERC20 supply becomes unbacked; contract's locked balance can be drained.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track per-user locked balances in `withdraw`/`deposit` instead of a shared contract-wide balance, and prevent re-deposit of tokens that were withdrawn by a different address.

hypotheses.title: Read-only reentrancy in FeeSplitter.totalSupply during Curves trade
hypotheses.description: `totalSupply(token)` computes `curves.curvesTokenSupply(token) - curves.curvesTokenBalance(token, address(curves))`. During a Curves `_transferFees` callback (attacker-controlled subject/referral), the attacker can reenter and call `FeeSplitter.addFees` (if manager) or trigger `onBalanceChange`, but more critically external integrators reading `totalSupply`/`getClaimableFees` mid-transaction see a transient state where `curvesTokenBalance[token][address(curves)]` has been updated by `withdraw`/`deposit` but the corresponding ERC20 mint/burn has not yet settled. An attacker contract can reenter `withdraw` (which calls `_transfer` to `address(this)` then `CurvesERC20.mint`) and during the `mint` callback (if the ERC20 were hookable) or during the ETH callback, read `totalSupply` to get a stale value and act on it.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker triggers a Curves trade that sends ETH to attacker contract. 2) In the callback, attacker calls `FeeSplitter.totalSupply`/`getClaimableFees` and observes a value computed from a partially-updated `curvesTokenBalance[token][address(curves)]`. 3) Attacker uses this stale value to compute an advantageous `addFees`/claim or to front-run a victim's claim within the same transaction.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect fee distribution / claim amounts; potential over- or under-claiming of holder fees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to Curves state-mutating functions and ensure FeeSplitter reads are only used after Curves state is fully settled (or expose a non-reentrant view).

hypotheses.title: deposit requires tokenAmount <= contract balance, blocking deposits after withdrawals
hypotheses.description: `deposit` requires `tokenAmount <= curvesTokenBalance[curvesTokenSubject][address(this)]`. The contract's balance of a subject only increases when users call `withdraw` (which transfers tokens to the contract). If all holders withdraw their ERC20 (or the contract balance is drained), no one can deposit back, because the check fails. This creates a one-way state where ERC20 tokens can be minted but never re-deposited.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker (or any user) calls `withdraw` for the full amount, moving all internal balance to the contract and minting ERC20. If the contract's internal balance is later reduced (e.g., via `deposit` by others), a subsequent depositor may find `tokenAmount > contract balance` and be unable to deposit, even though they hold the ERC20. More directly, if the contract balance is zero, no deposits are possible.
hypotheses.impact: ERC20 holders cannot convert back to internal tokens; their ERC20 becomes useless for depositing, effectively trapping value.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the contract-balance check or base it on the actual ERC20 supply held by the contract, ensuring deposits are always possible when the user holds ERC20.

hypotheses.title: No deadline or nonce on presale buys; startTime only gates opening
hypotheses.description: `PresaleMeta` has only `startTime`, `merkleRoot`, and `maxBuy`. There is no end time, so once `startTime` passes the presale remains open forever (the check is `startTime <= block.timestamp` reverts only before start). Combined with the reusable merkle proof, a whitelisted user can buy indefinitely.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until `startTime` passes. 2) Repeatedly calls `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted` with a valid proof, up to `maxBuy`. 3) Presale never closes, so the subject cannot transition to public sale cleanly.
hypotheses.impact: Presale never expires; whitelisted actors can accumulate tokens indefinitely, undermining intended sale windows.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an `endTime` to `PresaleMeta` and revert when `block.timestamp > endTime`.

hypotheses.title: FeeSplitter.totalSupply underflows when locked balance exceeds supply
hypotheses.description: `totalSupply` computes `curves.curvesTokenSupply(token) - curves.curvesTokenBalance(token, address(curves))`. The comment claims locked tokens are in the ERC20 contract, but `curvesTokenBalance[token][address(curves)]` is incremented in `Curves.withdraw` when users deposit into the ERC20 wrapper. If at any point the balance held by the Curves contract exceeds the total supply (which can happen because `withdraw` transfers balance to `address(this)` without reducing supply, and `deposit` transfers back), the subtraction underflows and reverts. This is reachable because `withdraw` moves tokens to `address(this)` while supply stays constant, and `deposit` moves them back — but if a user calls `withdraw` and the ERC20 mint fails or is not called, the balance at `address(this)` can exceed supply.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker calls `withdraw(subject, amount)` which transfers `amount` from their balance to `address(this)` and mints ERC20. If the ERC20 mint reverts (e.g., due to a malicious token or out-of-gas), the state is reverted. However, if a user transfers Curves tokens directly to `address(this)` via `transferCurvesToken(subject, address(this), amount)` — which is blocked by `ContractCannotReceiveTransfer` — so this path is blocked. The real risk is if `curvesTokenSupply` is reduced below `curvesTokenBalance[address(curves)]` via `sellCurvesToken` by the contract itself, which cannot happen. So this is a latent invariant risk.
hypotheses.impact: If the invariant is ever violated, `totalSupply` reverts, breaking `addFees` and all fee distribution, freezing holder fees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a checked subtraction with a clear revert, or track locked supply separately instead of deriving it from balances.

hypotheses.title: deposit/sellExternalCurvesToken ordering allows balance manipulation
hypotheses.category: Ordering / state update after external call
hypotheses.description: `deposit` calls `CurvesERC20(externalToken).burn(msg.sender, amount)` (external call) before `_transfer(curvesTokenSubject, address(this), msg.sender, tokenAmount)`. If `externalToken` is a malicious/upgradeable ERC20 (or if `msg.sender` is a contract whose `burn` triggers a callback — not possible with standard ERC20 but possible if the token is replaced), the attacker can reenter `deposit`/`withdraw`/`sellExternalCurvesToken` before the internal `_transfer` completes, causing double-counting of `curvesTokenBalance[curvesTokenSubject][address(this)]` and `curvesTokenBalance[curvesTokenSubject][msg.sender]`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker gets `externalCurvesTokens[curvesTokenSubject].token` set to a malicious ERC20 (via `_deployERC20` only deploys CurvesERC20, so this requires the factory to be malicious — but the factory is set by owner; if factory is trusted, this is not exploitable). 2) Attacker calls `deposit` with an amount; during `burn`, the malicious token reenters `deposit` or `withdraw`. 3) Attacker mints/burns multiple times against the same `curvesTokenBalance[curvesTokenSubject][address(this)]` before `_transfer` updates it.
hypotheses.impact: Double-spend of locked Curves tokens, inflation of ERC20 supply, drain of `address(this)` balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform `_transfer` before the external `burn` call, or add a reentrancy guard to `deposit`/`withdraw`/`sellExternalCurvesToken`.

hypotheses.title: buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted updates presalesBuys before merkle verification
hypotheses.description: `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted` increments `presalesBuys[curvesTokenSubject][msg.sender]` and checks `maxBuy` before calling `verifyMerkle`. If `verifyMerkle` reverts, the whole transaction reverts, so state is rolled back — but the ordering means an attacker can probe `maxBuy` limits and merkle proofs in a way that, combined with reentrancy from `_buyCurvesToken`'s `_transferFees` callback, allows the attacker to reenter `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted` and increment `presalesBuys` again before the outer call's `_buyCurvesToken` completes, bypassing `maxBuy`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is whitelisted with a valid proof. 2) Attacker calls `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted` with `amount` such that `presalesBuys` is just under `maxBuy`. 3) During `_buyCurvesToken` → `_transferFees`, ETH is sent to attacker (as subject/referral). 4) Attacker reenters `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted` with another `amount`; `presalesBuys` is incremented again and `maxBuy` check uses the already-incremented value, but the outer call's increment is not yet reflected in the inner call's view if ordering is off — or the inner call succeeds and the outer call also succeeds, exceeding `maxBuy`.
hypotheses.impact: Whitelisted buyer exceeds `maxBuy`, gaining more presale tokens than allowed; unfair allocation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `verifyMerkle` before `presalesBuys` update and add a reentrancy guard to `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted`.

hypotheses.title: transferAllCurvesTokens iterates ownedCurvesTokenSubjects with reentrancy risk
hypotheses.description: `transferAllCurvesTokens` loops over `ownedCurvesTokenSubjects[msg.sender]` and calls `_transfer` for each. `_transfer` calls `_addOwnedCurvesTokenSubject(to, ...)` which can push to `ownedCurvesTokenSubjects[to]`. If `to` is a contract that reenters `transferAllCurvesTokens` or `transferCurvesToken`, the array being iterated can be modified mid-loop, causing skipped entries or out-of-gas. Also, if `to == msg.sender` is not blocked (only `to == address(this)` is blocked), the loop can re-add subjects and grow unbounded.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `transferAllCurvesTokens(attackerContract)`. 2) During `_transfer`, `_addOwnedCurvesTokenSubject` pushes to `ownedCurvesTokenSubjects[attackerContract]`. 3) Attacker contract reenters `transferAllCurvesTokens` or `transferCurvesToken` to manipulate the array. 4) Loop skips tokens or reverts, leaving some tokens untransferred or causing DoS.
hypotheses.impact: Incomplete migration of tokens, potential DoS of `transferAllCurvesTokens` for users with many subjects.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard and/or snapshot the array length before the loop; block `to == msg.sender` if not intended.

hypotheses.title: Presale buy accounting updated before proof verification allows griefing/over-count
hypotheses.description: `presalesBuys[curvesTokenSubject][msg.sender] += amount` is executed before `verifyMerkle`. A caller who is not whitelisted can still increment their `presalesBuys` counter (the tx reverts on proof failure, so state rolls back — but a whitelisted user can pre-increment to the max with a valid proof, then be blocked from further buys). More importantly, the check `tokenBought > maxBuy` uses the cumulative counter, so a whitelisted user can be permanently capped by a single large buy, and the ordering means the counter is the sole gate rather than per-call amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Whitelisted attacker calls `buyCurvesTokenWhitelisted` with `amount = maxBuy` early. 2) Subsequent legitimate buys by the same address revert with `ExceededMaxBuyAmount`. 3) If `maxBuy` is per-address intended, this is fine; if per-call, it's a griefing vector against self only. The real issue is the counter is not reset and is not bound to a deadline.
hypotheses.impact: Whitelisted users can be locked out of further presale buys; no deadline means presale can be entered indefinitely once started.
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify the proof before mutating state, and add a presale end time / deadline to `PresaleMeta`.
